title: God, Creation and Providence
welcome_lead: Begin at the beginning: Christianity's doctrine of God as Creator and the providential ordering of history.

walkthroughs.body_html: Classical theism, articulated by Augustine, Anselm and Aquinas, ascribes to God omnipotence, omniscience, omnibenevolence, eternity, immutability, simplicity and aseity. Aquinas argues these attributes follow from God's being subsistent existence itself (ipsum esse subsistens). Process theologians like Charles Hartshorne dissent, holding God to be in some respects mutable and affected by creation.

The Lateran Council (1215) defined that God created 'from nothing' both spiritual and corporeal creatures. This contrasts with Plato's Timaeus (where the Demiurge shapes pre-existing matter) and with pantheistic emanation. Genesis 1, the Wisdom literature, and 2 Maccabees 7:28 form the biblical basis. Augustine's Confessions XI explores creation 'with' time rather than 'in' time.

Providence is general (the ordering of nature) and special (the guidance of individuals). The problem of evil, sharpened by Epicurus and Hume, asks how an all-good and all-powerful God permits suffering. Augustine's free-will defence and Hick's Irenaean 'soul-making' theodicy give two main Christian replies; Plantinga's free-will defence develops the logical version.

mcqs.q: What is the doctrine of the Trinity?
options: The Trinity refers to heaven, earth and hell.
Natural evil means evil that is good for nature.
Christians believe in three different gods.
God is one being existing in three persons (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) — distinct in person but united in essence; Christians remain monotheistic.
Aquinas's Five Ways are five Christian sacraments.
Aquinas's Five Ways are five steps of one cosmological argument.

Five distinct arguments for God's existence: from motion, causation, contingency, gradation of being, and final causes/teleology — collectively forming Aquinas's natural theology, not a single argument.
Natural evil means evil that is good for nature.

mcqs.q: What distinction matters for the free will defence to the problem of evil?
options: Natural evil means evil that is good for nature.
The free will defence solves all forms of evil at once.
Aquinas's Five Ways are five Christian sacraments.

Between moral evil (caused by free human choices) and natural evil (earthquakes, disease) — the free will defence directly addresses moral evil but struggles with natural evil, which isn't a product of free choice.
